title: Ethical Considerations for Generative AI
learners_amount: 48 learners have completed this activity in the past 12 months.
star_rating: Average rating of 4 stars by 4 learners in the past 12 months.
description:
About this learning activity

In this module, you’ll explore the fascinating and complex world of ethical considerations when creating content with generative AI. You’ll learn about the pillars of transparency, accountability, and fairness. You’ll discover ethical considerations and risks related to data inputs to AI tools and uncover the ethical implications of AI-generated output. Finally, you’ll explore the IBM AI risk atlas, an online resource that helps users understand some of the risks of working with generative AI, foundation models, and machine learning models.


What you will learn
At the end of this course, you will be able to:
 

  • Describe the ethical pillars of transparency, accountability, and fairness in the use of generative AI
  • Identify ethical considerations and risks related to data inputs in AI tools
  • Explain the ethical implications of managing AI-generated content


Lessons

  1. Ethics in the use of generative AI
  2. Managing the ethics of AI inputs for data
  3. Managing the ethics of AI-generated content
  4. Simulation: Exploring the IBM AI risk atlas

description:
About this learning activity

During this course, students will be able to put their theoretical knowledge into practice with hands-on use cases focusing on generative AI technologies. For the project, they will work in groups of 3 to 5 people. Together, they choose between one of several real-world business challenges from a company, tackle that use case, and present their solution at the end of the semester. Not only will students learn to work with generative AI tools and cloud services, but also how to efficiently and effectively combine them into a system. This is a cross-university course and will be offered at five universities simultaneously. Mixed groups are possible.
The semester is split into 2 parts: In the first part, there will be lectures to present the students with the necessary knowledge while the second part gives the students the time to specifically work on the project together. Q&A sessions will be offered to support the teams.

description:
About this learning activity

In this course, you’ll learn about AI governance and IBM’s comprehensive solution, watsonx.governance. You’ll follow the story of Anna Parker, a chief risk officer for an insurance firm, who wants to implement AI governance in her organization. The course outlines IBM’s methodical and phased strategy for setting up scalable and sustainable AI governance and AI model lifecycle governance. Watsonx.governance equips leaders like Anna to build a structured AI team, complete with dashboards, workflows, and automated risk alerts. By the end of this course, you’ll be able to explain the importance of AI governance, compare the risks of predictive versus generative AI, and outline the solutions IBM products offer to AI governance.

 

Earn a badge: Complete this course to earn an industry-recognized IBM digital credential called IBM watsonx.governance Technical Essentials.

 

Important: This course is offered on a different learning platform. To access it, you will need to sign up for an IBMid. Signup is easy, and there is no cost.

 

Audience: This course is intended for developers, data scientists, data analysts, and others who develop, deploy, or make decisions based on models in production, and who want to track the lifecycle of predictive models and govern AI-based projects.

 

What you’ll learn

After completing this course, you should be able to:

  • Explain the importance of AI governance
  • Identify the risks that are associated with predictive and generative AI-based projects
  • Outline the solutions IBM products offer to AI governance
  • Relate EU AI act articles to watsonx.governance capabilities
  • Use watsonx.governance to create and govern a generative AI-based project
  • Compare the risks of predictive versus generative AI

 

Units

  1. Introduction
  2. AI governance
  3. Governing foundation models
  4. Epilogue
